title: Szekely Goulash
subtitle: Hungarian braised pork with sauerkraut and soured cream
excerpt: Slow-braised pork shoulder cooked with sauerkraut, sweet paprika, caraway, and soured cream into a rich, tangy stew. A Transylvanian classic that eats like a whole meal in one pot.
sourceNotes: Transylvanian-Hungarian szekely gulyas tradition. Synthesised from multiple Hungarian and Central European culinary sources.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze without the soured cream. Stir in fresh soured cream when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well in a large pot. The flavour improves the next day.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook a day or two ahead. Reheat gently and stir in the soured cream just before serving.

content.text: Szekely goulash is a pork and sauerkraut stew finished with soured cream. The sauerkraut gives the dish its sharp character and cannot be swapped out. Rinse the sauerkraut only if it is very sour; a little sharpness is what the dish is built on.
Heat the oil in the dutch oven over a medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 12 minutes until soft and golden.
Take the pan off the heat. Add the paprika-sweet and paprika-hot. Stir quickly. Return to a low heat.
Add the garlic, caraway seeds, and tomato puree. Cook for 1 minute.
Add the pork pieces. Season with salt and black pepper. Stir to coat the pork in the paprika base. Cook for 5 minutes, turning the pork to colour it on all sides.
Add the sauerkraut, bay leaves, and stock. Stir well. Bring to a simmer, then cover and cook on a low heat for 75 minutes until the pork is very tender.
Mix the soured cream with the flour in a small bowl until smooth. Stir this into the stew. Simmer gently, uncovered, for 5 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Remove the bay leaves. Taste and adjust salt. Serve with boiled potatoes and scatter with parsley.

items.cause: The sauerkraut was very sharp and not drained well.
items.fix: Rinse the sauerkraut under cold water before adding. A pinch of sugar can also balance the acidity.

items.symptom: The soured cream split and looks grainy.
items.cause: It was added to boiling liquid, or the flour was not mixed in.
items.fix: Always mix the flour through the soured cream before stirring it in. Add it to a gently simmering stew, not a rolling boil.

items.symptom: The pork is still tough after an hour.
items.cause: The heat was too high, or the pork was not a shoulder cut.
items.fix: Turn the heat to the lowest setting and cook for a further 20 to 30 minutes. Pork shoulder needs time to soften properly.
